tldr: PrimeSim is an action-conditioned multiview world model simulator built on a pretrained video generator. By combining midtraining on over 30,000 hours of robot demonstrations with four-stage posttraining, it runs at 10.1 FPS and supports long-horizon reinforcement learning policy improvement.
hero_caption: Overall overview of PrimeSim. (a) A diverse robot demonstration dataset of roughly 30,000 hours collected across 22 platforms, (b) a model architecture that takes a unified action representation and multiview video as input and performs autoregressive 4-step generation after posttraining, and (c) results demonstrating strong benchmark performance, adaptation to unseen embodiments, and application as a policy evaluation and training simulator.
overview:
Reinforcement learning and data collection on real physical robots always come with risks of hardware damage and massive time costs. On the other hand, manually engineered physics simulators face heavy manual modeling burdens and a significant reality gap (Sim-to-Real gap). Video-generation-based world models have attracted attention as an alternative, but to truly serve as a simulator, three capabilities are essential: faithfully following robot actions, maintaining geometric consistency across camera views, and sustaining coherent long-horizon rollouts without collapsing when feeding self-generated images back as inputs.

This study presents PrimeSim, a robot simulator that addresses these challenges. First, using a pretrained video foundation model (Wan2.2-TI2V-5B) as the starting point, the authors conducted midtraining on 30,110 hours of demonstration data spanning 22 robot platforms. They mapped diverse robot motions into a unified 31-dimensional action representation, introduced frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strictly align frames and actions temporally, and developed view-aware interleaved attention to balance view-specific representations with cross-view information exchange. Next, through posttraining, they sequentially applied an autoregressive structural transformation, 4-step causal consistency distillation, self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching distillation against a bidirectional teacher, and a hierarchical KV cache temporal memory.

In experiments, PrimeSim achieved fast generation at 10.1 FPS on a single A100 GPU and sustained stable long-horizon rollouts lasting up to 105 seconds. It also showed high transferability, adapting to unseen robot embodiments within just 100 to 200 gradient steps, and demonstrated sufficient fidelity to support GRPO-based reinforcement learning policy optimization entirely inside the simulator.
contributions: Established a progressive training framework that transforms a pretrained video generation model into an interactive robot simulator with action conditioning and multiview consistency.

Constructed a large-scale corpus spanning 22 platforms and 30,110 hours of demonstration data, and developed a unified action representation across heterogeneous embodiments, frame-aligned dual-path conditioning, and view-aware interleaved attention.

Integrated causal consistency distillation, self-rollout training with asymmetric distribution matching, and hierarchical temporal memory in posttraining, simultaneously achieving fast inference (10.1 FPS) and mitigating error accumulation during long-horizon self-generation.

Set top-tier performance on WorldSimProbe and EWMBench, and demonstrated that policy evaluation and GRPO reinforcement learning training inside the generated environment transfer faithfully to a physics simulator.

sections.heading: Why video generation models need to be retooled into simulators
sections.summary: World models that render the visual outcomes of policy actions can serve as safe, parallelizable simulators, but merely producing plausible video is not enough. A viable robot simulator simultaneously requires faithful action following, multiview consistency across viewpoints, and stability over long-horizon autoregressive rollouts.
sections.details:
In reinforcement learning for autonomous robot skill acquisition, hardware damage and massive sample collection costs from trial-and-error on physical machines are constant obstacles. Meanwhile, manually engineered physics simulators suffer from an inherent Sim-to-Real gap. Consequently, using world models that predict future observations conditioned on policy actions as simulators has long been explored.

However, even video generation models capable of synthesizing natural-looking videos cannot be directly deployed as robot simulators. A true simulator faces three stringent requirements:
- The robot and environment must faithfully move according to commanded actions (Action Following).
- Arm and object spatial relationships must remain geometrically consistent across multiple cameras, such as head and wrist views (Multiview Consistency).
- Errors must not explode over long-horizon loops when the model's own past imperfect generations are fed back as the next inputs (Long-Horizon Coherence).

PrimeSim resolves these requirements through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained backbone, the model learns physical dynamics from 30,110 hours of heterogeneous robot data across 22 platforms, followed by fast generation and self-rollout training to build a practical simulator.

sections.heading: Building a pipeline to unify 30,000 hours of heterogeneous robot data
sections.summary: By integrating open-source and proprietary datasets, the authors built a 30,110-hour robot demonstration corpus spanning humanoids, bimanual setups, single-arm robots, UMI handheld devices, and simulators. A four-stage processing pipeline filters video quality, detects action anomalies, aligns sampling rates and camera counts, and transforms data into a unified action space.
sections.details:
Recent approaches often rely on vast collections of cheap egocentric human videos for pretraining, but geometrically aligning human hands with robot end-effectors requires complex processing. In this work, recognizing that open and proprietary robot demonstration datasets have already reached substantial scale, the authors directly pooled robot demonstrations and mapped them into a shared action space.

To construct the training corpus from raw data, they designed the following four-stage pipeline:

### Stage 1: Video Quality Filtering
Optical flow measures motion magnitude between frames. Clips with minimal movement are filtered out to prevent bias from static frames, using platform-specific thresholds tailored to wrist versus static cameras. Frames with heavy JPEG compression artifacts and extremely short clips under one second are also discarded.

### Stage 2: Action Quality Filtering
Complex mechanisms that make up only a tiny fraction of the corpus, such as multi-fingered hands and bipedal locomotion, are excluded for simplicity (wheeled humanoids are retained). Data with sharp action discontinuities from sensor glitches or missing values unrecoverable via forward kinematics (FK) are removed.

### Stage 3: Data Alignment
All sequences are resampled to 10 Hz, and camera viewpoints are standardized to three views (e.g., head, left wrist, right wrist). Missing camera slots are filled by duplicating the primary camera. Natural language instructions are generated from metadata templates when missing, and data is stored in the LeRobot format.

### Stage 4: Action Alignment
When only joint positions are provided, forward kinematics via URDF compute end-effector poses, with rotations unified into quaternions $(x,y,z,w)$. Furthermore, actions are converted into relative action chunks anchored to the first frame of each window as the origin, neutralizing differences across platform coordinate frames.

captions.F3: Statistics of the training corpus. Totaling 30,110 hours and 2.38 billion frames, with an 84:16 ratio of real-world to simulated data, covering a wide range of task categories and diverse embodiments such as wheeled humanoids, bimanual arms, single arms, and UMI.

sections.heading: PrimeSim architecture and the design of midtraining and posttraining
sections.summary: Starting from the Wan2.2 video foundation model, midtraining introduces a unified action representation, dual-path conditioning, and multiview attention. Posttraining then turns the model into a simulator through causal autoregression, 4-step consistency distillation, asymmetric distribution matching self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Pretrained Backbone
The model adopts weights from Wan2.2-TI2V-5B as its foundation, leveraging its pretrained visual and motion priors over real-world object permanence, textures, and lighting environments.

### 3.2 Midtraining
To inject robot control and multiview awareness into the video model, the authors integrate the following components and train using conditional latent flow-matching loss:
- **Unified Action Representation**: A 31-dimensional vector accommodates 6-DoF end-effector poses, gripper states, head/waist/torso joint positions, and base planar velocities $(v_x, v_y, \omega)$ (Figure F5). Converting to relative representations $\tilde{a}_{t+i|t} = a_{t+i} \ominus a_t$ anchored to the window's first frame absorbs coordinate frame discrepancies.
- **Frame-Aligned Dual-Path Conditioning**: Standard cross-attention often struggles with which frame corresponds to which action. PrimeSim uses a shifted diagonal attention mask where frame $t$ attends strictly to action $a_{t-1}$, alongside an adapter path that directly injects action features into frame tokens, ensuring tight control.
- **View-Aware Interleaved Attention**: Across 30 DiT blocks, two blocks apply attention strictly within individual camera views, while every third block applies global cross-view attention across all three views. Prepending unique camera identity tokens to each view's tokens preserves view-specific resolution while enforcing cross-view geometric consistency.

### 3.3 Posttraining: Fast-Video, Slow-Memory
The midtrained bidirectional model offers high quality, but running it as an autoregressive simulator requires too many inference steps (50 steps) and suffers from exposure bias when conditioning on past outputs. A four-stage posttraining pipeline overcomes this with a fast-video, slow-memory design:
- **Stage 1 (Causal Adaptation)**: Chunk-causal attention is introduced so the model autoregressively generates future frames conditioned solely on past chunks.
- **Stage 2 (Causal Consistency Distillation)**: Causal consistency distillation compresses the 50-step local ODE trajectory into a 4-step sampler, making self-rollout training computationally feasible.
- **Stage 3 (Clip-Level Self-Rollout with Asymmetric DMD)**: The model rolls out sequences using its own past generated frames via the KV cache. Using the frozen midtrained bidirectional model as an asymmetric teacher via distribution matching distillation (Asymmetric DMD), it prevents mode-averaging blur while boosting robustness to self-generated artifacts.
- **Stage 4 (Episode-Level Adaptation with Hierarchical Temporal Memory)**: Rollouts scale to complete episodes. The KV cache is structured into three tiers—a global sink for initial anchor frames, a slow macro memory storing thinned long-term history, and a dense local memory for recent frames—keeping memory footprint constant while maintaining coherence over 100 seconds.

captions.F5: Unified action representation defined in PrimeSim. Dedicated slots for head, torso, waist, dual end-effector poses, dual grippers, and mobile base velocities handle varying platform degrees of freedom via zero-padding.

sections.heading: Simulator performance evaluation and reinforcement learning validation
sections.summary: PrimeSim outperformed competing open-source models on standard benchmarks and achieved 10.1 FPS inference on a single A100 GPU. It showed strong transferability to unseen robots and environments, and GRPO reinforcement learning conducted entirely inside PrimeSim substantially boosted policy success rates on a physical simulator.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Benchmark Comparisons and Inference Throughput
- **WorldSimProbe**: Evaluating environmental responsiveness to commanded actions across five open-source action-conditioned world models, PrimeSim led on four of five suites: global trajectory coverage (T2: 67.9), behavior preservation (T3: 72.3), interaction dynamics (T5: 37.1), and interaction grounding (T4: 85.7). It ranked second only to LingBot-VA on local action calibration (T1: 70.2 vs. 77.0), indicating room for improvement in fine-grained control.
- **EWMBench**: PrimeSim took first place overall with an aggregate score of 6.09 across eight axes, clearly surpassing the previous state of the art, GE-Sim (LTX variant at 5.82).
- **Inference Speed**: On a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (bfloat16), PrimeSim processed a 3-view, 33-frame window ($288\times 384$ resolution) in 3.16 seconds, delivering 10.12 TempFPS (30.35 ViewFPS), well ahead of GE-Sim 2.0 (6.73 ViewFPS) under matching 4-step distillation conditions.

### 4.2 Adaptation to Unseen Embodiments and Environments
Few-shot adaptation was evaluated on three held-out platforms (xArm 7, ALOHA ViperX 300, and UMI gripper). While the baseline pretrained backbone failed to generate coherent motion even after 2,000 steps, PrimeSim's midtrained model mastered action-following video generation within just 100 to 200 gradient steps (Figure F7). On the unseen XVLA cloth-folding dataset with novel camera setups and backgrounds, it showed strong zero-shot following and accurately captured fabric deformation dynamics with 200 fine-tuning steps (Figure F8).

### 4.3 Long-Horizon Rollouts and Memory Ablations
In extended autoregressive rollouts up to 105 seconds (1,046 frames), Stage 4 episode-level training and hierarchical temporal memory reduced image degradation from initial frames ($\Delta$PSNR) from 8.43 dB down to 6.01 dB.

### 4.4 Validation as a Policy Simulator
In the LIBERO-Spatial environment, PrimeSim predicted success rates across eight OpenVLA policy checkpoints with perfect rank ordering relative to ground-truth physics simulator results (Spearman rank correlation $\rho = 1.00$, Pearson correlation $r = 0.99$). Furthermore, running 200 steps of GRPO (Group Relative Policy Optimization) reinforcement learning entirely inside PrimeSim—using rollout frames and a simple learned reward classifier without physics simulator access—boosted policy success rate on the ground-truth physics simulator from 61.7% to 73.2%, proving that policy improvements inside the world model transfer to physical dynamics.

captions.F7: Few-shot adaptation to unseen platforms. The top row shows PrimeSim (midtrained) generating coherent, action-following motion in just 100 to 200 steps, whereas the bottom row shows the pretrained backbone failing to learn appropriate motion even after 2,000 steps.

sections.heading: Evolution of video generation and interactive world models in robotics
sections.summary: Video generation models have evolved from early data augmentation tools and visual backbones into action-conditioned interactive world models predicting environment transitions. Originating in gaming, this trajectory is now expanding into robotics simulators where multiview consistency and continuous physical control take center stage.
sections.details:
The application of video generation in robotics has advanced through two major phases:

### Early Days of Video Generation in Robotics
Initial works primarily used video models for data expansion on scarce teleoperation datasets, synthesizing visual trajectories to alleviate the shortage of physical robot data. Later efforts extracted the spatiotemporal physical understanding acquired through large-scale pretraining, using video models directly as visual representation backbones for planning and policy learning.

### Shift to Interactive World Models
Recently, focus has shifted toward interactive world models that accept agent actions as inputs and respond dynamically in real time. While this direction originated in video games and virtual environments, applying it to robotics introduces distinct demands:
- Continuous, physically grounded control signals must be faithfully reflected rather than discrete symbolic keystrokes.
- Geometric consistency must be sustained across multiple camera perspectives, including egocentric and third-person views.
- Physical validity in contact and deformation matters far more than mere visual plausibility.

PrimeSim tackles these robot-specific challenges head-on, stepping beyond game-like interactions to deliver the fidelity needed for actual policy learning.

sections.heading: Summary of findings and open challenges for world model simulators
sections.summary: PrimeSim advances video foundation models into robot simulators, demonstrating action following, inference throughput, and reinforcement learning policy optimization. At the same time, the authors note limitations: a modest 192×256 resolution, the need for few-shot gradient steps on unseen robots, and pending verification on physical robot hardware.
sections.details:
### Summary
This study introduced PrimeSim, which transforms video foundation models into a causal, multiview simulator for robotic manipulation. Through midtraining on over 30,000 hours of cross-embodiment demonstrations and posttraining spanning causal adaptation, consistency distillation, asymmetric DMD, and hierarchical memory, it reconciles 10.1 FPS execution with faithful action conditioning. Its fast adaptation to unseen platforms and successful policy improvement via in-model GRPO mark a meaningful milestone toward learned simulators.

### Limitations and Future Work
The authors candidly highlight several constraints:
- **Resolution limits**: The evaluated model generates views at $192\times 256$ resolution, prioritizing physical fidelity as a simulator over high-resolution pixel realism.
- **Zero-shot embodiment transfer**: While adapting to held-out platforms takes only 100 to 200 steps, it is not yet fully zero-shot. Expanding training scale and refining action representations remain future directions.
- **Physical hardware verification**: Closed-loop policy evaluations and GRPO training in this work were validated against a physics simulator (LIBERO) as ground truth. Evaluating whether policies trained inside PrimeSim deploy successfully onto physical hardware remains to be confirmed.

takeaways: Turning video generators into simulators requires more than naive fine-tuning: attention designs enforcing temporal frame-action alignment and posttraining tailored for self-generation loops (self-rollout plus asymmetric DMD) are critical.
Expressing actions relative to the first frame of each window neutralizes coordinate origin discrepancies, serving as a key enabler for cross-embodiment training.

Pairing 4-step consistency distillation with hierarchical KV cache management simultaneously achieves real-time inference above 10 FPS on a single GPU and long-horizon stability exceeding 100 seconds.
GRPO reinforcement learning using only world model rollouts and a simple reward classifier can measurably boost policy performance on an external physics simulator.
limitations: Generation resolution is relatively low at $192\times 256$, limiting precise rendering of fine-grained contacts and detailed tool tip geometry.
As shown by WorldSimProbe, fine-grained local action calibration (T1) trails macroscopic trajectory following, leaving room for improvement in sub-centimeter responses.
Transferring to completely unseen robot platforms requires 100 to 200 gradient adaptation steps rather than achieving true zero-shot generalization.
Validation of policies trained inside the world model remains confined to a physics simulator (LIBERO), leaving direct Sim-to-Real transfer to physical robot hardware unverified.
